title: Hybrid probe-and-fallback mediator for early-output commit and model routing
creator: Priya Nambiar
description: Goal: implement a lightweight mediator in the runtime that coordinates a short 'probe' prefill on a fast model/kernel and decides whether to commit to its early tokens or fallback to a thorough decode on a higher-fidelity path. This ticket scopes the routing policy, acceptance signalling, and graceful fallback behavior so product traffic can benefit from faster responses without increasing error surface or cache inconsistency.
proposal_summary: Introduce a Probe-and-Commit mediator that: 1) issues a fast, constrained prefill (probe) on an affine kernel/model variant; 2) computes an acceptance score from compact signals (logit gap, token entropy delta, cross-model agreement heuristic, kernel-affinity score); 3) if acceptance >= threshold, commit and stream early tokens; otherwise perform a full decode on the nominated fallback path. Ensure KV cache and streaming consistency by tagging probes and enabling rollforward heartbeat for soft fallbacks.
design_decisions: Use a short-duration prefill window (prefill tokens <= 8) to limit wasted compute on fallbacks.

Acceptance signal will be a weighted linear combination of: logit-margin, top-k agreement with slower model probe (when available), and a kernel-affinity penalty to avoid kernels known to hallucinate on certain sequence lengths.
Probe runs on a low-latency kernel/quantized variant with strict timeout; fallback uses standard kernel/full-precision model variant.

Fallback behavior is 'soft-fallback' by default: stream probe tokens immediately but attach a validation flag; if final decode disagrees beyond threshold, issue a corrected suffix and record metric for rollback rate.
Implement routing policies as config objects so product teams can opt into aggressive commit (higher user-perceived latency gains) or conservative commit (lower rollback rate).
tradeoffs: Aggressive acceptance thresholds improve latency and token cost but increase rollback/correction events which are visible to end users and complicate analytics.
Running cross-model agreement checks improves quality but costs extra compute and increases probe tail latency — only enable for high-value routes.
Tagging streamed probe tokens simplifies UX for corrections but requires client-side handling changes; we prefer server-side correction messages for backward compatibility.
Maintaining KV cache consistency across probe and fallback paths adds complexity: we'll use namespace tagging and a short-lived probe-cache that can be merged if commit succeeds.
Implementing kernel-affinity scoring increases scheduling complexity but lets us avoid known pathological kernels for certain sequence lengths or ops.
implementation_steps: Define Probe API surface (timeout, max_prefill_tokens, kernel_hint, acceptance_threshold).
Implement lightweight acceptance scorer component in runtime with pluggable signal sources.
Add probe-cache namespace and merge-on-commit semantics to KV cache layer.
Wire mediator into request path: prefill -> score -> commit/stream or fallback decode path.
Instrument telemetry: probe_latency, acceptance_score_distribution, rollback_rate, extra_tokens_emitted, probe_compute_cost.
Add config flags and route-level policy toggles; expose conservative/aggressive presets in Console later.
End-to-end tests including streaming correctness, rollback messaging, and cache merge/cleanup.
Prepare RFC and API docs, and a developer guide for how SDKs should consume correction messages.
acceptance_criteria: Median p95 latency improvement on targeted low-cost routes >= 15% with default conservative policy.
Rollback rate (probe commits later corrected by fallback) <= 1.5% for conservative policy and <= 5% for aggressive policy in canary traffic.
No KV cache leakage after probe-fallback cycles; probes' temporary cache entries cleaned within 30s if not committed.
End-to-end streaming clients receive either a single consistent token stream or a clearly-delimited correction message; backwards-compatible behavior verified.
Telemetry is available in Console for acceptance_score histograms, rollback traces, and per-route cost delta.
testing_plan: Unit tests for acceptance scorer with synthetic signals covering edge cases (e.g., low entropy but small logit gap).
Integration tests: simulate probe success/failure and validate KV cache merge/rollback semantics.
Chaos tests: introduce artificial probe timeouts and kernel failures to validate fallback determinism.
A/B canary: 1% traffic using conservative policy then ramp to 10% if metrics meet targets.
Evaluate on representative workloads: short chat completions, instruction-following prompts, and long-context summarization to surface pathological patterns.
rollout_plan: Canary on internal services first (beta console, internal CI bots). Phase 1: conservative policy for non-critical routes (1% -> 10% over 2 weeks). Phase 2: enable cross-model agreement checks for selected high-value routes and expose aggressive preset behind runtime flag; monitor rollback and customer impact metrics before broader ramp.
